extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and patent office examiners dealing with inventions involving biological material (microorganisms/biological samples)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive requirements across jurisdictions for depositing biological material (microorganisms, cultures, other biological samples) in support of patent applications, including what must be deposited, where, timing, storage duration, access conditions, undertakings, and required notifications. Covers Budapest Treaty and national/alternative deposit arrangements and access restrictions (expert-only, experimental-use undertakings, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: A sample of biological material must be deposited if the carrying out of the invention involves the use of biological material which is neither available to the public nor describable in the patent application in such a manner as to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictions consistently state that if an invention concerns biological material not publicly available or not fully describable in the application, the description is inadequate unless the material has been deposited with a recognized depositary. Some states (e.g. Germany) treat a valid deposit as making the description sufficient for patentability. France requires the description to specify information available to the applicant on characteristics of the microorganism and the authorized body and deposit number. References: Patents Acts/Regulations and Budapest Treaty conformity noted throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit with an international depositary authority (Budapest Treaty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposit shall be made with an international depositary authority under the Budapest Treaty or with another depositary authority recognized by the relevant patent office or EPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many offices (Finland, Iceland, Estonia, Czech, Hungary, etc.) require deposits with an IDA under the Budapest Treaty; WIPO publishes recognized depositaries. Some countries (e.g. Germany) permit an alternative 'recognized scientific institution' deposit outside the Budapest Treaty subject to specified guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative deposit outside Budapest Treaty (recognized scientific institution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions allow depositing biological material outside the Budapest Treaty with a 'recognized scientific institution' that must guarantee storage and furnishing according to national rules and be independent of the applicant/depositor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germany: applicant may choose either deposit under the Budapest Treaty or deposit outside it with a recognized scientific institution that is legally, economically and organisationally independent of the applicant. Such non‑Budapest deposits must meet national ordinance requirements (e.g., irrevocable declaration of release, storage period, furnishing rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof/documentation of deposit and notification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must furnish documentary proof of the deposit (deposit certificate/number) and, in many jurisdictions, inform the patent office of the depositary name and deposit/access code within a specified time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Czech practice requires proof attached to the application; Finland and Iceland require the applicant to inform the patent office in writing of the depositary and access code within 16 months from filing or priority date (or when requesting early publication). Germany requires documentary evidence for third‑party deposits. Where PCT applications are involved, information may be filed with WIPO/IB within the same time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of Deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: The biological material must be deposited not later than the date of filing of the patent application (or the priority date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most jurisdictions mandate deposit on or before filing/priority date (Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, etc.). A few earlier entries (e.g., Cuba entry referencing harmonization) showed different phrasing; any jurisdictional variance should be checked locally. Finland and others reiterate deposit no later than filing date; proof/information about the deposit may be submitted within 16 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for reporting deposit information (16‑month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant shall inform the patent office in writing of the name of the depositary authority and the access code given to the deposit within 16 months from the filing date or, where priority is claimed, from the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finland, Iceland and other jurisdictions explicitly require submission of deposit details within the 16‑month window; if the applicant requests early publication, the information must be submitted when making that request. For PCT applications, the same information may be filed with WIPO/IB within the same time limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of Storage (Budapest Treaty Rule 9.1 / national minima)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposited biological material shall be stored in accordance with the Budapest Treaty: generally five years after the most recent request for furnishing a sample and in any event for at least thirty years from the date of deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple national entries cite Rule 9.1 (five years after last furnishing request and, in any case, 30 years). France states minimum duration of storage is 30 years. Germany explains the Budapest-storage rule and special rules for non‑Budapest deposits (e.g., five years from last request and at least another five years after expiry of max statutory IP term for non‑Budapest deposits). Georgia says stored during the term of validity of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of Availability of Samples (when samples become available)
rubrics_metrics.description: Samples of deposited biological material become available from the date on which the patent application is made available to the public (publication/laying open), typically 18 months from filing or priority date, except where applicant requests earlier disclosure or other special conditions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finland, Denmark, France, Germany, Iceland and others specify availability from publication (18 months) or earlier if the applicant furnishes a copy. Rule 11 of the Budapest Treaty governs furnishing conditions. National laws may add authorized‑person access pre‑publication in certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑publication access to samples for authorized persons / file inspectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Up to publication, access to the deposited biological material may be provided only to persons authorized under national law to inspect files (or as authorized under international treaties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hungary and Greece state that up to publication, access is limited to those authorized to inspect files. National rules determine who is 'authorized'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's option to restrict furnishing to independent experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant may request that, until a patent has been granted (or for a specified period after refusal/withdrawal), samples shall be furnished only to an independent expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many jurisdictions permit an 'expert option' (Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland). Typically the applicant must notify the patent office before publication preparations are completed or within a statutory time limit (often within the 16‑month window). If an application is refused/withdrawn, some jurisdictions (e.g., Finland, Denmark, Greece, Hungary, Iceland) allow the expert‑only restriction to continue for 20 years from filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on use and onward transfer by requester (undertakings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person supplied with a sample must undertake not to make the sample or any material derived from it available to third parties and to use the sample only for experimental purposes until patent rights have expired or the application is finally decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary and others require written undertakings: do not communicate the culture or derived material to others, use only for experimental purposes (except where compulsory/ex officio license applies), and, in some cases, undertakings must be attached to the furnishing request. Derived materials retaining essential characteristics are covered by the same undertaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and filing of requests for samples / required declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for furnishing samples must be filed in writing with the patent authority and include declarations/undertakings to observe restrictions on use; if the sample is to be furnished to an expert the expert may give the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iceland, Finland, France, Denmark and other entries require written requests and declarations. If sample is to be furnished to an expert, either the requester or the expert (as specified) must provide the undertaking. National procedural rules and Rule 11 of the Budapest Treaty apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrevocable declaration of release for non‑Budapest deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a deposit is made outside the Budapest Treaty, the applicant must issue an irrevocable declaration of release making the deposited biological material available without reservation to the depositary institution from the date of filing until the end of the storage period for issuing samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germany specifically requires an irrevocable declaration of release for non‑Budapest deposits; evidence of availability must be supplied for third‑party deposits. The purpose is to ensure the depositary can furnish samples per national rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert qualification and lists / applicant‑approved experts
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'expert' is a person acceptable to the applicant or approved by national rules; some offices publish lists of experts and applicants may nominate or approve experts for expert‑only access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finland defines an expert as a person who has declared willingness and whose name is included in a list of experts published by the National Board, though the applicant may also approve another person. Rules for who qualifies as an independent expert vary by jurisdiction and are set out in national law or ministerial rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and procedure if deposit ceases to be available
rubrics_metrics.description: If the biological material deposited ceases to be available from the recognized depositary authority, a new deposit should be made under the Budapest Treaty and a signed statement certifying equivalence of the newly deposited material must be filed with the patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greece (and other national provisions) require re‑deposit under the Treaty terms and filing a depositor's statement confirming the newly deposited material is the same as originally deposited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑grant availability of samples
rubrics_metrics.description: After grant of the patent, samples of the deposited material shall be furnished upon request to any person; during the patent term the requester remains subject to undertakings restricting use and onward transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germany, Hungary and others specify that after grant, samples are available to anyone; obligations not to make material available and to use it only for experimental purposes continue to apply (subject to compulsory licenses). National law may also address availability after revocation/cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific national durations or special rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions specify particular storage/availability rules or durations beyond Budapest minimums (e.g., France: minimum storage 30 years; Georgia: store during patent validity; Denmark: expert‑only supply can be requested to continue for 20 years after filing if application refused/withdrawn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of country‑specific deviations and additional procedural steps (e.g., Denmark: requests and declarations to observe restrictions filed with Patent Authority; France: conditions and undertakings governed by national code articles; Germany: different treatment for Budapest vs non‑Budapest deposits). Always consult the national provision cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer/Change of depositary (notification obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a deposited sample is transferred from one international depositary to another, the applicant must inform the patent office as soon as possible after receiving receipt for the transfer, providing the new deposit number and depositary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iceland explicitly requires notification to the patent office after transfer under Rule 5.1 of the Budapest Regulations; patent offices may request a copy of the deposit receipt.
